title: Long-Context Generalization with Sparse Attention
claim: Our adaptive-temperature sparse attention keeps accuracy high at sequence lengths far beyond training, while dense and fixed-temperature baselines degrade.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, log-x sequence length, shaded in-distribution region
description: Two line charts sit side by side. Both plot accuracy against sequence length on a log-scaled x-axis. A grey shaded band labeled 'In-Distribution' marks the training lengths at the left of each plot. The left chart shows exact-match accuracy from 32 to 65K tokens. Its curves are Softmax+RoPE (black dashed, which collapses almost immediately), Softmax+NAPE and Entmax+NAPE (dashed green and purple, which drop around 8K to 16K), SSMax+NAPE (solid green, which drops later), and ASEntmax+NAPE (solid purple, which stays near 100%). The right chart shows accuracy from 16 to 4K with seven methods, including Softmax, Adaptive Temperature, Top-K, SSMax, Entmax with alpha 1.5 and 16, and ASEntmax. Colors and line styles separate the methods. The solid purple ASEntmax line stays on top and decays the slowest. The legends are inside or beside the plots.
caption: Long-context generalization on Multi-query Multi-token Associative Recall (left) and Max Retrieval (right). SSMax represents the Scalable Softmax approach by [ref], and Adaptive Temperature (Adapt. Temp.) represents the approach by [ref]. While all methods benefit from using NAPE (NoPE + ALiBi), our adaptive-scaling version of $\alpha$-entmax exhibits the best extrapolation results, effectively handling extremely long sequences.
abstract: Transformer-based architectures traditionally employ softmax to compute attention weights, which produces dense distributions over all tokens in a sequence. While effective in many settings, this density has been shown to be detrimental for tasks that demand precise focus on fixed-size patterns: as sequence length increases, non-informative tokens accumulate attention probability mass, leading to dispersion and representational collapse. We show in this paper that dynamically sparse attention mechanisms using $Î±$-entmax can avoid these issues, due to their ability to assign exact zeros to irrelevant tokens. Furthermore, we introduce Adaptive-Scalable Entmax (ASEntmax), which endows $Î±$-entmax with a learnable temperature parameter, allowing the attention distribution to interpolate between sparse (pattern-focused) and dense (softmax-like) regimes. Our empirical evaluation on synthetic tasks and language modeling demonstrates that ASEntmax substantially outperforms softmax, scalable softmax, and fixed-temperature $Î±$-entmax baselines, achieving up to 1000$\times$ length extrapolation on synthetic benchmarks and superior long-context generalization on language modeling while preserving short-context performance, including better perplexity trends and higher retrieval accuracies at 8$\times$ training length.
